notes:
I've written notes for all 23 verses, but the research is uneven. My search limit ran out before I could reach several sources you asked for. Everything below comes from pages I actually read: Guzik (Enduring Word), Ellicott, Gill, Calvin, Matthew Henry, Precept Austin and Bible Hub's combined commentary pages.

**What's missing:**
- **Catholic and Orthodox writers in their own words.** Nothing from newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org. The purgatory reading of v. 15 appears below only as Protestant writers describe it, so it shouldn't go into the commentary as the Catholic view until checked against a Catholic source.
- **Modern scholarship.** No NET Bible notes or bibleodyssey.org. Gordon Fee appears once, and only as quoted by Guzik.
- **Traditions' own teachers.** Nothing from Wesleyan, Lutheran, Pentecostal or Baptist denominational sites, and nothing on the "carnal Christian" debate from desiringgod.org or gty.org.
- **Popular modern teaching** (prosperity, word of faith, hyper-grace): none found.

So section 2 below shows where commentators disagree, not tradition-by-tradition positions. Where a Bible Hub page combines several commentators and I couldn't tell who wrote a passage, I left it out.

---

## 1. The traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1:** Guzik: the Corinthians are "brothers" and have the Spirit, unlike the natural man of 2:14. Yet they act fleshly, like baby Christians. He separates *sarkinos* ("made of flesh," ordinary human weakness) from *sarkikos* ("marked by the flesh," able to do better but not doing it), which is the word here. He sees three kinds of people: natural, spiritual and carnal. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-3/
- Ellicott: Paul means they really *were* carnal, not that he spoke as if they were. Here "carnal" just means the opposite of spiritual, not gross sin. "Babes" is the opposite of the "mature" of 2:6. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/3.htm
- Gill: they weren't unregenerate. They thought and acted in fleshly ways, and the flesh still had strong control of them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-corinthians-3.html
- Matthew Henry: believers are only partly sanctified and still need to grow. The Corinthians were proud of their knowledge even though they were still babes. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Cr/1Cr_003.cfm

**v. 2:** Guzik: Paul stuck to the basics because they thought they were ready for "deeper things" they weren't living. Milk and solid food differ in degree, not kind. There aren't two gospels, and nothing should be held back. Their trouble was a taste for "spiritual junk food," meaning human wisdom and eloquence. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-3/
- Ellicott: Paul doesn't blame them for being babes at first. He blames them for not growing. Their complaint that his teaching was too basic was really their own fault. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/3.htm
- Gill: the "milk" is the plain, easy teachings of the gospel, not "the milk of the law." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-corinthians-3.html
- Pulpit Commentaries: the Corinthians complained that Paul was too simple, but he knew what they needed. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-corinthians-3.html

**v. 3:** Guzik: their divisions prove they're fleshly. Problems with people show problems with God. Paul says they *behave* like mere men, not that they *are* unsaved. He quotes Fee: staying worldly isn't one of the options. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-3/
- Ellicott: "walking in the way of man" means a merely human way of living, not a Spirit-taught one. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/3.htm
- Gill: some Syriac readings say "ye are in the flesh," but Paul doesn't mean the unregenerate state. Their envy and quarrels made them hard to tell apart from people with no religion. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-corinthians-3.html
- Precept Austin (quoting MacArthur): in 1:18–2:16 the division came from love of human wisdom. In 3:1–9 it comes from giving in to the flesh. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-3-commentary

**v. 4:** Ellicott: the Paul and Apollos parties stand for all the factions. Paul rebukes his *own* fans to show he isn't jealous for himself. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/3.htm
- Guzik makes the same point: Paul condemned his own fan club rather than enjoy their praise. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-3/
- Gill: the Corinthians preferred Apollos for his eloquence, and another group scorned all ministers. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-corinthians-3.html

**v. 5:** Guzik: you believed *through* these men, not *in* them. He quotes Maclaren on the pointlessness of arguing over which of "two nothings" was greater. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-3/
- Ellicott: the questions are deliberately blunt: "What is Apollos?" Ministers are only tools God used as he chose, so making them party leaders is absurd. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/3.htm
- Calvin: no one should be boasted in, because faith allows boasting only in Christ. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/1-corinthians-3.html
- Gill: ministers are servants, not lords or founders of sects. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-corinthians-3.html

**v. 6:** Ellicott: Paul founded the church and Apollos taught it afterwards, which fits Acts 18:1, 18:27 and 19:1. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/3.htm
- Guzik: farmers don't make things grow, only God does. "Planted" and "watered" describe finished acts, while "gave the growth" describes God's ongoing work. Workers should be content with the job God gives them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-3/

**v. 7:** Ellicott: "is anything" means "is anything worth mentioning," as in Galatians 6:3. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/3.htm

**v. 8:** Guzik: everyone is on one team, but each is rewarded for their own labour, not their gifts or success. He quotes Hodge: a faithful worker in obscurity may be rewarded above those with great results. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-3/
- Ellicott: the ministry has both unity and individuality. Men should see the unity, and God alone judges the differences. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/3.htm

**v. 9:** Ellicott: "God" comes three times for emphasis. The picture switches from farming to building because building can be developed further. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/3.htm
- Guzik: it's amazing that God wants us as working partners. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-3/
- Matthew Henry: we work under God, with him and for him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Cr/1Cr_003.cfm

**v. 10:** Ellicott: opening with "by the grace" keeps "expert builder" from sounding like boasting. "Someone else" covers Apollos and others after him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/3.htm
- Matthew Henry: Paul was a wise master-builder, but grace made him one. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Cr/1Cr_003.cfm
- Calvin: the more the Corinthians belittled Paul, the higher he states his calling. Later builders must build to match the foundation. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/1-corinthians-3.html
- Precept Austin: "be careful" is a present-tense command, meaning keep weighing how you build. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-3-commentary

**v. 11:** Guzik: Christ is the only foundation, laid when Paul founded the church (Acts 18). A church not built on him isn't a church, though people can build badly on the right foundation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-3/
- Ellicott: the foundation, the person of Jesus Christ, can't be changed or added to. The care is about the materials built on it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/3.htm

**v. 12:** Ellicott:
- "Precious stones" means fine building stone like marble, not gems. Hay filled gaps in walls, and straw made thatched roofs.
- Paul was picturing marble palaces next to wood-and-straw shacks when a city fire breaks out.
- He warns against reading each material as a particular doctrine or virtue. The point is lasting work versus passing work, aimed mainly at teachers.

https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/3.htm
- Guzik: gold, silver and stone recall the materials of the Jerusalem temple (1 Chronicles 22, 29). Mixing human wisdom with God's is like building in alternate layers of straw and marble. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-3/
- Gill takes the materials as the doctrines a minister teaches. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-corinthians-3.html

**v. 13:** Ellicott: the "Day" is the Lord's coming, pictured as bursting in with fire (Malachi 3–4, 2 Thessalonians 1:8). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/3.htm
- Guzik: the fire tests what *sort* the work is, not how much. He quotes Moody: converts should be weighed as well as counted. He links it to the judgment seat of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-3/
- Precept Austin: only the Lord grades work, and it isn't believers' job to grade each other. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-3-commentary

**v. 14:** Ellicott: good builders are rewarded by their work surviving the fire. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/3.htm

**v. 15:** Guzik: some will be "barely saved," with everything gone and no crown to give Jesus (Revelation 4:10–11). The fire tests the *work*, not the worker. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-3/
- Bengel (on Bible Hub): the loss is of reward, not salvation. Paul pictures a shipwrecked merchant who survives but loses his cargo. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_corinthians/3-15.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: "the ship is lost, the sailor saved," like a brand snatched from the fire (Zechariah 3:2). It is a comfort that sincere but weak workers are still saved. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_corinthians/3-15.htm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: salvation is a free gift, not a reward, so it can't be the thing lost. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_corinthians/3-15.htm

**v. 16:** Guzik: the stress is on the whole church as temple, with individuals coming in 6:19. *Naos* means the inner sanctuary where God lives, not the wider temple area. The earthly temple was the picture and the church is the reality. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-3/
- Ellicott: "Do you not know" suggests their behaviour showed they had forgotten. A holy temple suggests the precious materials stand for spiritual qualities. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/3.htm

**v. 17:** Ellicott: read "destroy" rather than "defile," the opposite of building up. Death was the penalty for violating the old temple (Exodus 28:43), so God won't let the destroyer of his spiritual temple go unpunished. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/3.htm
- Barnes and the Cambridge Bible: it is the same Greek verb in both halves, so "if anyone destroys… God will destroy." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_corinthians/3-17.htm
- Guzik: how we treat the church matters to God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-3/

**v. 18:** Guzik: Paul is being sarcastic, since the Corinthians did think themselves wise. They must give up man-centred wisdom even if people call them fools. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-3/
- Ellicott: Paul returns to the problem of exalting teachers. Human wisdom is worthless for spiritual purposes, so it's no reason to exalt a teacher. Become a fool in the world's eyes. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/3.htm
- Precept Austin (quoting Kistemaker): worldly wisdom shows up in people who want to run their own lives rather than submit to Christ. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-3-commentary

**vv. 19–20:** Ellicott: one proof text is from Job and one from the Psalms. Apart from James 5:11, this is the New Testament's only reference to Job. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/3.htm
- Guzik: God has judged worldly wisdom to be foolish, crafty and futile. Will we agree? https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-3/

**v. 21:** Ellicott: stop party spirit, because teachers exist for you, not you for them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/3.htm
- Guzik: saying "I follow Paul" is too narrow, when everything is yours in Christ. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-3/

**v. 22:** Guzik: even death is our servant, like the angel freeing Peter in Acts 12. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-3/
- Precept Austin: we should be glad for and learn from all the faithful leaders God sends. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-3-commentary

**v. 23:** Ellicott:
- Believers own everything because Christ owns them.
- "Christ belongs to God" may be added so the "Christ party" can't claim the line for themselves.
- It refers to Christ as Mediator and doesn't deny his full divinity.

https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/3.htm
- Guzik: "All are yours" is Christian liberty, and "you are Christ's" is Christian responsibility. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-3/

---

## 2. Where interpreters differ

**vv. 1–3: Is there such a thing as a "carnal Christian"?** Guzik notes the debate. Some say it's a contradiction and these people weren't Christians. He answers that Paul calls them brothers and babes in Christ. He accepts Redpath's line that the carnal Christian is saved but "traveling third class." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-3/ He also quotes Fee: staying worldly isn't an option (same URL). Gill and Matthew Henry also treat them as truly born again but still fleshly (Gill URL above; https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Cr/1Cr_003.cfm). I found no source on the other side.

**v. 13: What are the "Day" and the "fire"?**
- Ellicott and Guzik: the Lord's return and final judgment. (URLs above)
- Gill: *not* the Day of Judgment, but a time of trial in this life, such as persecution or error, that tests a minister's teaching. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/3-13.html
- Calvin: the fire is a metaphor for the touchstone that tests teaching. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/1-corinthians-3.html

**vv. 12–15: Whose work is tested?**
- Mainly teachers: Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/3.htm), JFB and Gill, who make it a minister's teaching (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_corinthians/3-15.htm).
- Guzik: first leaders, then all God's servants. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-3/

**v. 15: What is the "loss"?**
- Lost reward, salvation kept: Bengel, JFB, Pulpit (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_corinthians/3-15.htm).
- Barnes: a lower rank in heaven that lasts forever. Not misery, but knowing one might have had more. (same URL)
- Matthew Poole: loss could come now, through God's discipline or lost reputation. "Saved as through fire" is a proverb for scraping through. (same URL)
- Gill: loss of his labour and of the praise he hoped for. (same URL)
- Calvin: such builders are saved *on condition* that the Lord clears away their ignorance and purges their dross. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/1-corinthians-3.html
- Cambridge Bible: sincerity doesn't prove the teaching right, but it saves the person. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_corinthians/3-15.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: rejects a reading by some Church Fathers that the workman is kept alive to suffer endless torment. (same URL)

**v. 17: Who does God destroy, and how?** A Precept Austin passage, with the author unnamed in what I read, takes the destroyer to be an unbeliever. It contrasts him with the believer in vv. 13–15, whose *work* burns while he is saved. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-3-commentary Ellicott only says God will punish him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/3.htm

---

## 3. Other views

**v. 15 and purgatory (described by Protestant critics only):**
- Guzik says Roman Catholics use this verse for purgatory. He calls it a human invention that denies Christ's finished work, and stresses the fire tests work, not the worker. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-3/
- Ellicott: "as if" shows the fire is a metaphor. Forgetting that, Roman theologians built purgatory on these words. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_corinthians/3.htm
- Matthew Poole: the purgatory reading fails because that fire would cleanse only lesser ("venial") sins, while this fire tests everyone's work, gold included. Gill also rejects it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_corinthians/3-15.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/3-13.html
- A Bible Hub Q&A argues several points against it. Works are judged, not souls. "As" marks a comparison, not a place. Believers are already washed and justified (6:11). It also says purgatory was formally defined only at Lyon (1274), Florence (1439) and Trent (1563). https://biblehub.com/q/1_Cor_3_15_s_link_to_purgatory.htm
